passages.happening:
Samuel speaks to all Israel at Gilgal. He has listened to them and set a king over them. ‘Now here is the king walking before you, and I am old and gray’ (verse 2).

Then he asks them to judge him. “Here I am. Bear witness against me before the LORD and before His anointed: Whose ox or donkey have I taken? Whom have I cheated or oppressed? From whose hand have I accepted a bribe and closed my eyes? Tell me, and I will restore it to you” (verse 3).

“You have not wronged us or oppressed us,” they replied, “nor have you taken anything from the hand of man” (verse 4). Samuel calls the LORD and the king as witnesses that they have found nothing in his hand, and the people answer, ‘He is a witness’ (verse 5).
passages.hearers:
This is Samuel's speech at the ceremony at Gilgal that ends chapter 11. He does not retire. He will keep praying and teaching, and he will confront Saul twice in the chapters ahead. But he hands over the leadership that judges like him had carried.

He opens in the language of a court. He calls the LORD and the new king as witnesses, lists the usual abuses of a powerful man, taking an ox or a donkey, cheating, oppressing, taking a bribe to look the other way, and invites anyone to bring a claim.

The list answers Samuel's warning in chapter 8, where he said that a king would take and take. The contrast is sharp. The old judge took nothing. The new king will be tempted to take everything.
passages.later:
Moses had made the same claim when his leadership was challenged: “I have not taken one donkey from them or mistreated a single one of them” (Numbers 16:15).

Paul, saying goodbye to the elders of Ephesus, said the same of his own work among them: “I have not coveted anyone’s silver or gold or clothing” (Acts 20:33).
passages.asks: Samuel could ask the whole nation whether he had taken anything, and no one could answer. Ask what people would say if you asked them the same question. And ask whether there is anything you have taken that you need to give back.

passages.t: The LORD's righteous acts, and the terms
passages.happening:
Samuel reminds them of what the LORD has done. ‘Now present yourselves, so that I may confront you before the LORD with all the righteous acts He has done for you and your fathers’ (verse 7).

When their fathers cried out in Egypt, the LORD sent Moses and Aaron and brought them out (verse 8). But they forgot the LORD, and he gave them into the hands of Sisera, the Philistines and the king of Moab (verse 9). They cried out and confessed that they had served the Baals and Ashtoreths, and the LORD sent Jerubbaal, Barak, Jephthah and Samuel to rescue them (verses 10-11).

Then, when Nahash the Ammonite came against them, they asked for a king, ‘even though the LORD your God was your king’ (verse 12). “Now here is the king you have chosen, the one you requested. Behold, the LORD has placed a king over you” (verse 13).

Samuel sets out the terms. “If you fear the LORD and serve Him and obey His voice, and if you do not rebel against the command of the LORD, and if both you and the king who reigns over you follow the LORD your God, then all will be well” (verse 14). But if they rebel, the LORD's hand will be against them as it was against their fathers (verse 15).
passages.hearers:
This is a covenant speech, like the farewells of Moses in Deuteronomy and of Joshua near the end of his book. It follows a familiar pattern: a review of what God has done, a charge with a promise and a warning, a sign, and a renewed commitment.

It is built like a trial. First Samuel is cleared. Now the LORD's righteous acts are laid out, and the people are shown to be in the wrong. In verse 7 the word righteous acts means God's faithful deeds of rescue. In this speech righteousness means God doing right by his people.

Samuel's review squeezes the book of Judges into a few lines. Jerubbaal is Gideon's other name. Where the Berean Standard Bible has Barak, the traditional Hebrew text reads Bedan, a name not otherwise known as a judge; the BSB follows the Greek and the Syriac. Some ancient versions also read Samson instead of Samuel in verse 11. These are small questions about the text, and they do not change the point of the speech.

The terms in verses 14 and 15 sit at the center of the chapter. The king is under the same covenant as everyone else. Israel's kingship can only last if the king himself serves Israel's true King.
passages.later: The book of Judges gives the same pattern in one line: ‘Then the LORD raised up judges, who saved them from the hands of those who plundered them’ (Judges 2:16). It explains Gideon's other name: ‘So on that day Gideon was called Jerubbaal’ (Judges 6:32).
passages.asks: Samuel told the story of God's faithfulness before he gave the warning. Ask what righteous acts of God you would list from your own life. And ask whether remembering them changes how you hear his commands.

passages.t: Thunder at harvest, and a promise to pray
passages.happening:
“Is it not the wheat harvest today? I will call on the LORD to send thunder and rain, so that you will know and see what a great evil you have committed in the sight of the LORD by asking for a king” (verse 17). Samuel calls, and the LORD sends thunder and rain that day, and all the people greatly fear the LORD and Samuel (verse 18).

They beg him, “Pray to the LORD your God for your servants so that we will not die! For we have added to all our sins the evil of asking for a king” (verse 19).

“Do not be afraid,” Samuel replied (verse 20). They have done wrong, but they must not turn away from the LORD. They are to serve him with all their heart, and not turn after ‘worthless things that cannot profit you or deliver you, for they are empty’ (verse 21). “Indeed, for the sake of His great name, the LORD will not abandon His people, because He was pleased to make you His own” (verse 22).

“As for me, far be it from me that I should sin against the LORD by ceasing to pray for you. And I will continue to teach you the good and right way” (verse 23).

He ends with a charge and a warning: fear the LORD and remember what great things he has done, ‘But if you persist in doing evil, both you and your king will be swept away’ (verse 25).
passages.hearers:
The sign would have struck a farmer hard. The wheat harvest came in late spring and early summer, in the dry season, when rain is almost unknown in the land of Israel. Rain then could ruin grain lying cut in the fields. Thunder and rain at harvest were plainly not ordinary weather. In a land where Baal was worshiped as the storm god who gave the rain, the sign also said who really commands the sky.

Samuel turns from prosecutor to intercessor. He does not take back what he said: asking for a king was evil. But he will not abandon them, and he will not stop praying. He treats ceasing to pray for them as a sin against the LORD. Praying for the people is part of his office, and it goes on after they have set him aside.

The word for worthless things is the word used in Genesis 1:2 for the formless earth. Here it means idols: empty, unable to save. To turn from the LORD is to turn toward nothing.

The covenant rests on God's own commitment, ‘for the sake of His great name’. Yet it still carries real conditions. The chapter ends not with comfort but with the warning repeated, so that it closes with weight.
passages.later:
A proverb shows how strange rain at harvest was: ‘Like snow in summer and rain at harvest, honor does not befit a fool’ (Proverbs 26:1).

A psalm makes Samuel's promise its own: “For the LORD will not forsake His people; He will never abandon His heritage” (Psalm 94:14).
passages.hard:
If asking for a king was a great evil, why did God give them one? And why does the Bible later honor David and the coming king?

The difficulty is real, and the books of Samuel hold both sides on purpose. The law of Moses had already looked ahead to a king and set limits on him, so kingship itself was not forbidden. What Samuel condemns is the motive. Israel wanted a king ‘like all the other nations’ (8:5), and when Nahash threatened, it turned to a human ruler instead of the LORD who had saved it again and again.

Some scholars see two strands in 1 Samuel, one favorable to the monarchy and one critical of it, set side by side by an editor. Others read the tension as one deliberate argument. Either way, the picture is the same. A king is good only when he is himself under God's rule. God grants the request, turns it to his own purpose, and later promises David a lasting house. The sin lay in the demand, not in the office.
passages.asks: Samuel said that to stop praying for the people would be a sin. Ask whom you have stopped praying for, perhaps someone who set you aside. And ask what it would mean to keep teaching ‘the good and right way’ to people who did not take your advice.
